transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Moore (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Li (NimbusHealth - Platform), Sofia Reyes (NimbusHealth - ML infra), Jorge Alvarez (NimbusHealth - CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to tune throughput for NimbusHealth inference workloads. Focus areas: continuous batching window, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, burst_slots), token ceilings/limits, KV cache prefetch and prewarm, straggler mitigation strategies, and on-prem/VPC numering and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps include running targeted benches and sharing environment access and docs.

Topics covered:
- Continuous batching heuristics and sequence packing
- max_num_seqs and its interplay with token_limit / token_ceiling
- KV cache prefetch / prewarm, eviction policies
- Straggler mitigation: per-req priority and soft timeouts
- Quantization (int8/int4) impact on throughput and tail latency
- On-prem/VPC considerations: NUMA, device contention, pinned GPU pools

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Ethan: hey everyone good afternoon, thanks for joining, uh we set aside an hour to get into the knobs that affect throughput for your workload. i'm Ethan from Redwood, and with me is Priya our infra se.
[00:00:22] Mark: thanks Ethan, appreciate it. i'm Mark, i run the platform team at NimbusHealth. we see high variance during peak hours, tail latency spikes, and we think batching/config might help.
[00:00:36] Priya: awesome, yeah we'll walk through continuous batching, scheduler knobs and also some prefetch/kvcache ideas. quick question, what model family are you running for the prod workload?
[00:00:48] Sofia: it's a ~7B open family, quantized to int8 for cost. sequences are usually short but we have spikes: some threads run 600-1200 tokens for summarization.
[00:01:02] Jorge: important to note we have an on-prem cluster behind a VPC for PHI. can't send traffic to hosted right now. whole thing is isolated.
[00:01:14] Ethan: great context. we'll keep the discussion VPC/on-prem centric then. starting with continuous batching: for workloads where you have a large proportion of short sequences, continuous batching with a tight prefetch window can greatly improve GPU utilization.
[00:01:30] Priya: the key knobs we tune are: max_num_seqs, batch_window_ms, burst_slots and token_limit. max_num_seqs caps the number of concurrent sequences packed into a single step; batch_window controls latency vs packing.
[00:01:48] Mark: can you give concrete starting values? we've been using defaults and seeing a lot of small batches.
[00:01:56] Priya: start with max_num_seqs=32 for your 7B-int8, token_limit 1024, and batch_window_ms 30-50ms. if latency SLO is 200ms p95, you might push batch_window to 50ms to let the scheduler gather more requests.
[00:02:12] Sofia: we have a hard p95 of 250ms. does increasing max_num_seqs risk tail latency?
[00:02:20] Priya: yes it can. two ways to handle: 1) per-request priority so interactive requests bypass packing or 2) soft timeouts where stalled sequences are force-evicted before they block the batch. we also have a token_ceiling setting to prevent very long sequences from holding the batch.
[00:02:40] Jorge: token_ceiling vs token_limit - what's the distinction? i've seen both in docs.
[00:02:46] Ethan: good callout. token_limit is per-request maximum we accept at the API layer; token_ceiling is a scheduler-side guard used during packing to keep batches homogeneous and bounded so one long seq doesn't blow past memory. some people conflate them.
[00:03:02] Mark: about k-v cache - we've observed cold-cache penalties on long conversations. any prefetch strategies?
[00:03:10] Priya: yes, k-v prefetch or prewarm: if you can supply a short context prefix in the request, the runtime can precompute and prime the KV cache for the model. Redwood has a kv_preheat option in on-prem runtime that accepts a prefix snapshot and warms the GPU caches. note: on quantized int4 kernels prewarming behavior is slightly different due to kernel selection.
[00:03:34] Sofia: we're worried about memory pressure when prewarming. what eviction policies are recommended?
[00:03:40] Priya: LRU with size-based eviction is usually good. we expose kv_cache_max_bytes and kv_cache_eviction_ttl so you can bound memory. for on-prem, tune kv_cache_max_bytes to a fraction of GPU memory (e.g. 30-40%) leaving headroom for activations.
[00:03:58] Mark: can you explain how max_num_seqs interacts with kv cache hitrate?
[00:04:04] Priya: sure — larger max_num_seqs increases packing and amortizes the kernel launch overhead but may mix sessions with low cache affinity; that can reduce kv hitrate if sequences are from different conversations. a pattern we've seen: aggressive packing + prefetch per-session gives best throughput if you can tag session IDs and prewarm per-session.
[00:04:26] Ethan: also consider affinity-based scheduling: pin high-affinity sequences to specific slots so their kv cache warms and stays hot.
[00:04:34] Jorge: how do we measure affinity? by session id?
[00:04:38] Priya: yes session id or user id. scheduler can use a soft affinity weight so the same GPU gets requests from the same session preferentially. that's in the advanced scheduler flags.
[00:04:48] Mark: about stragglers — we see a few requests that take 2-3x longer and drag p99. what's the recommended mitigation?
[00:04:56] Priya: three practical levers: 1) per-request soft-deadline/eviction where if a sequence exceeds its step time it's evicted and retried on next slot; 2) watchdogs that detect slow kernels (often NUMA/CUDA issues on on-prem) and restart the worker; 3) isolate long-running requests via priority lanes so they don't block the fast lane.
[00:05:18] Sofia: numerics — we've experienced CUDA kernel slowdowns when device memory fragmented. any pro tips for on-prem?
[00:05:24] Priya: pre-allocating buffers and using pinned GPU pools helps. also ensure the runtime uses the right kernel variants: kernel selection is based on seq length distribution, quantization mode and hardware (SM count). mis-selection can cause catastrophic slowdowns. we recommend uploading a small profiling snapshot to let the runtime pick kernels.
[00:05:44] Ethan: to the profiling point, we'd like to run a targeted bench on your cluster. Priya, can you outline what we'll need?
[00:05:50] Priya: we need a representative request trace: sequence length histogram, arrival rate, and the session ids distribution. also GPU topology: number of GPUs, memory per GPU, NUMA grouping, and whether MIG or MPS is in use. ideally a short synthetic load generator spec.
[00:06:06] Mark: we can provide that. for the bench we want to test: max_num_seqs values [8,16,32,64], token_limit [512,1024,2048], batch_window_ms [20,50,100], and with/without kv_preheat.
[00:06:20] Priya: perfect — we'll also test burst_slots toggles and priority lanes. expected outcomes: throughput curves, tail latency, kv hitrate, GPU utilization and memory usage.
[00:06:32] Jorge: what's the typical tradeoff when increasing max_num_seqs? we want more throughput but not at the expense of p99.
[00:06:38] Priya: typical pattern: throughput increases sublinearly with max_num_seqs because of seq packing inefficiencies and kv miss penalties. p99 can worsen if a few long sequences dominate. That's where token_ceiling and priority lanes help.
[00:06:54] Mark: any heuristics for adaptive windows? we have diurnal spikes and sudden bursts.
[00:07:00] Priya: use adaptive batch_window_ms that's workload-aware: increase batch_window during sustained high qps to pack more, but lower it during spikes. Redwood's runtime has an adaptive_batching mode that monitors queue depth and RPS slope. you can also use burst_slots to allow transient spikes to be absorbed without growing max_num_seqs globally.
[00:07:20] Ethan: can we talk about quantization interactions? Sofia mentioned int8. what if they go to int4 to save cost?
[00:07:28] Priya: int4 reduces memory and increases throughput on supported kernels but kernel selection becomes narrower and some fused kernels for attention are different. int4 sometimes increases p99 because of less optimized kernels for longer seq. measure both. also int4 may change prewarm footprint for kv.
[00:07:44] Sofia: do you support mixed quantization profiles per-customer? we might want critical flows in int8 and bulk in int4.
[00:07:50] Ethan: yes, Redwood supports model variants and can route by policy. you can keep a higher-quality variant for interactive flows and a lower-cost variant for batch. routing is transparent via model aliases.
[00:07:59] Mark: about the scheduler knobs — are they hot-reloadable on on-prem? we prefer not to restart everything.
[00:08:04] Priya: most scheduler knobs are hot-reloadable: max_num_seqs, batch_window_ms, token_ceiling, burst_slots. Changes apply per worker gradually. Some changes to kernel selection require model reloads, but that's separate.
[00:08:18] Sofia: can we instrument per-customer kv hitrate?
[00:08:21] Priya: yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route and per-session KV hitrate, plus token-level cost breakdowns. for on-prem we ship a local collector that reports to your S3 or inside VPC.
[00:08:34] Mark: curious — you mentioned soft eviction earlier. how do you avoid losing partial progress for users?
[00:08:40] Priya: we evict only at step boundaries and mark partials as retryable. When a sequence is evicted mid-generation we preserve the KV snapshot if safe so on retry it can resume faster. This is a tradeoff: sometimes retaining partials costs memory. We expose an evict_policy: immediate, preserve_partial, snapshot+reclaim.
[00:09:00] Jorge: security concerns — does kv prewarm leak data if sessions from different tenants share a GPU?
[00:09:06] Ethan: good question. for multi-tenant on-prem we recommend per-customer GPU pinning or tenant isolation. Redwood's KV cache supports namespace isolation; prewarm can be restricted to tenant-scoped contexts. We also support KMS integrations for keys at rest.
[00:09:22] Sofia: what about audit logs for evictions and prewarm operations?
[00:09:26] Ethan: on-prem distribution includes audit logging hooks. every prewarm, eviction and kernel restart is emitted with timestamps and session ids to the local audit stream.
[00:09:36] Mark: earlier you mentioned NUMA problems. can we detect and auto-correct?
[00:09:40] Priya: runtime exposes GPU-locality metrics. for instance, cross-NUMA memcpy spikes show up in the telemetry. we have a NUMA watchdog that can throttle or migrate workloads if it detects repeated memcopy stalls. In worst cases it will restart the worker.
[00:09:56] Jorge: for the bench, do you want us to simulate real arrivals or replay logs?
[00:10:00] Priya: both. replaying logs gives realistic seq packing and session affinity. synthetic spike tests help test burst_slots behavior. please provide at least 15 minutes of representative logs plus a spike script.
[00:10:12] Mark: let's cover expected outputs of the bench — what will you deliver?
[00:10:16] Priya: we'll deliver a spreadsheet: throughput @ various configs, p50/p95/p99 latencies, kv hitrate, GPU utilization, memory pressure, and suggested knob settings per SLO. We'll also include recommended model variant config if int4/int8 tradeoffs matter.
[00:10:30] Ethan: timeline — Priya can run the bench once we get access; aim for results by next week.
[00:10:36] Jorge: sounds good. one more question — fallback policies, if a GPU is saturated can the runtime fallback to hosted or other region?
[00:10:44] Ethan: with Redwood Private you can configure remote fallback policies but in your case with PHI you may want strict private-only. If you have hybrid mode, runtime can fallback to a pre-approved variant in another region but this requires data residency checks.
[00:10:58] Mark: okay — let's talk about a specific failure mode we saw last month: a rapid spike caused eviction storms and then a cascade of kernel restarts. any diagnosis tips?
[00:11:06] Priya: eviction storms usually come from a badly configured token_ceiling or aggressive prewarm that runs out memory. The cascade of kernel restarts often means the watchdog saw repeated CUDA errors. Steps: capture core dumps, upload the small profiling trace we talked about; we'll look for OOM, kernel launch retries, and memcopy latencies.
[00:11:24] Sofia: i can attach logs. do you need driver versions?
[00:11:27] Priya: yes driver, CUDA, cuDNN/oneDNN versions, and any custom kernel patches. Also whether MIG is enabled.
[00:11:36] Ethan: let's pivot to tuning plan: 1) baseline run with your current config; 2) sweep max_num_seqs and token_limit; 3) test kv_preheat and eviction policies; 4) test adaptive batching and burst_slots. Priya will run or provide instructions.
[00:11:54] Mark: who owns the run? we can give you access or we'll run locally and upload traces.
[00:11:58] Priya: best if you give us limited access to a test node. we can run non-invasive benches and share the toolchain. if not, provide the trace and we'll give command-line scripts you can run.
[00:12:10] Jorge: about metrics — what exact graphs should we expect in the console?
[00:12:14] Priya: p50/p95/p99 latency over qps, tokens/sec, kv hitrate, batch_size histogram, max_num_seqs distribution, kernel selection heatmap, GPU util + memory used, and error/call-failure rates.
[00:12:26] Mark: perfect. two quick micro-questions: 1) if we set max_num_seqs=64 and batch_window_ms=100, will that blow up memory on 80GB GPUs? and 2) what's a safe kv_cache_max_bytes fraction?
[00:12:38] Priya: 1) It depends on avg seq length; worst-case memory is roughly sum of activations for the packed sequences. For 7B int8, 64 sequences with long tokens can spike memory; start with smaller numbers and monitor OOM. 2) kv_cache_max_bytes start at 30% GPU mem, increase if you have headroom, but monitor allocations.
[00:12:56] Sofia: are there quick flags to limit memory blowup during tests?
[00:13:00] Priya: enable token_ceiling=1024, kv_cache_eviction_ttl=300s, and set a per-request token_limit. also enable the runtime's OOM soft-guard which rejects new large requests when free mem is low.
[00:13:14] Mark: great. any gotchas for on-prem VPC networking? we saw occasional request duplication.
[00:13:20] Ethan: duplication can be from retries at load balancer level. add idempotency keys and ensure front-door timeouts are longer than scheduler batch_window. Also ensure the LB doesn't resend on partial connections.
[00:13:34] Jorge: last question: do you have any recommended default for priority lanes?
[00:13:38] Priya: allocate 5-10% of slots as latency-priority for interactive requests. use affinity to keep those warm. For example burst_slots=8, priority_slots=4. Tune based on observed fraction of latency-critical traffic.
[00:13:54] Mark: ok — this is useful. let's confirm next steps and owners.
[00:13:58] Ethan: recap: Priya will run the bench (or provide scripts) with the sweep we discussed and produce the spreadsheet; Mark will provide access/logs and GPU topology; Ethan will send security docs and the benchmark template. Delivery targets: Priya results by 2026-10-28, Mark access by 2026-10-25, Ethan docs by 2026-10-22.
[00:14:22] Jorge: thanks all.
[00:14:24] Mark: thanks team.
[00:14:26] Ethan: closing notes: we'll also include a short note on kernel selection and a quick checklist for mitigating eviction storms.
[00:14:34] Sofia: appreciated.
[00:14:36] [Call ends — rest of the 58 minutes were Q&A and narrow config clarifications; logs and follow-ups exchanged offline]
